sentences.text: Estimates based on related taxa suggest Vivaron grew to between 12 and 18 feet in length.
It can be distinguished by two prongs on the posterior part of the maxilla where it meets the jugal bone.
Comparisons with related taxa estimate a length of approximately 3.5 to 5 meters, similar to other rauisuchids.
The genus was named in 2016 based on fossils collected at Hayden Quarry in 2009.
The species name honors John Hayden, the hiker who discovered the quarry in 2002.
It is debated whether Postosuchus also possessed a fifth alveolus, as a reconstruction by Long and Murry (1995) possibly shows one on the left premaxilla.
Vivaron is classified as a member of the Rauisuchidae family based on a phylogenetic analysis by Lessner et al. in 2016.

The presence of Vivaron in the southwestern United States, alongside Postosuchus, implies that many other rauisuchid fossils from that region previously assigned to Postosuchus kirkpatricki require morphological re-analysis.
The type species of the genus Vivaron is Vivaron haydeni.
Vivaron lived during the Late Triassic (middle Norian) in the Chinle Formation of New Mexico.
Vivaron lived during the Norian stage of the Triassic, between 227.3 and 205.7 million years ago.
There are three recorded fossil occurrences of Vivaron in the Paleobiology Database.
